extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, judges, and other patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the two-step Alice/Mayo framework to determine whether patent claims are directed to patent-ineligible subject matter (abstract ideas) and whether the claims contain an inventive concept that renders them patent-eligible. Focuses on claim characterization, claim language vs. specification, ordered-combination analysis, and related procedural presumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the two-step framework set forth by the Supreme Court in Mayo and Alice: (1) determine whether the claim is 'directed to' a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea); (2) consider the elements of each claim individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether the additional elements 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application (a search for an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Mayo Collaborative Servs. v. Prometheus and Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank as the governing test. At step one ask what the claim is directed to; at step two examine whether claim elements (alone or combined) add significantly more than the ineligible concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate claim characterization at step one
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize the claim based on its language and the functions it recites (do not overgeneralize or misstate the claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The district court’s characterization should reflect the claim terms (e.g., 'A computer-implemented method for decoding a transmission signal' comprising steps of receiving, deinterleaving, combining, and decoding). A party's rephrasing that is not meaningfully different from the claim language does not show error. Do not import unclaimed limitations to alter the directed-to inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract-idea examples: data operations and information processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to receiving, manipulating, encoding/decoding, gathering, or combining data are within the realm of abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent identifies encoding/decoding and gathering/combining data as abstract (citing Hawk Tech, RecogniCorp, Digitech). If the core functions are generic data handling steps, step one likely finds an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely invoke generic processes and machinery (e.g., 'using a computer processor' or otherwise do not require specialized hardware) are more likely to be abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim fails to disclose specific means or methods and instead recites generic computer implementation, that supports a finding of abstraction (Two-Way Media). A requirement for a 'specialized computer' can distinguish eligible claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental steps / pencil-and-paper indicia of abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: If claimed methods can be performed in the human mind or using pencil and paper, that is a 'telltale sign' of abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether claimed operations are basic cognitive tasks or simple arithmetic that a person could perform unaided (PersonalWeb). Such capability militates toward finding an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting to particular content or field does not avoid abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely limiting an abstract idea to a particular content (e.g., a particular type of information) or field of use does not render the claim less abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Elec. Power Grp. and Affinity Labs: restricting an abstract idea to a particular technological environment or particular content does not by itself make the claim patent-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement-in-functionality requirement for computer-technology claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as a patent-eligible improvement, claims must be directed to an improvement in the functionality of the computer or network platform itself, not merely to applying an abstract idea in a technological field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Customedia: show that the claim improves computer or network functionality itself (e.g., a new way the computer operates), rather than just an abstract idea implemented on a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive-concept analysis of ordered combinations at step two
rubrics_metrics.description: At step two, consider whether the elements individually or in combination provide an 'inventive concept' that transforms the abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely reciting the ineligible concept plus conventional steps is insufficient. If the asserted benefits are not tied to the particular ordered combination claimed (or the specification shows the same benefits for different orders), the order does not supply an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on unclaimed specification details to supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Technological details disclosed in the specification but not captured in the claim language cannot be used to supply the inventive concept necessary for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Intell. Ventures, Am. Axle, and ChargePoint: the specification cannot be used to import additional details or performance benefits into the claims when those details are not claimed. Evaluate inventive concept based on the claim as written.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements known in the prior art or routine/mental operations do not supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: If claim elements (other than the alleged inventive step) were used in the prior art, or if the alleged inventive step is basic arithmetic/mental operations, those cannot supply the inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify prior art usage of claimed steps. Basic combining/averaging or arithmetic that can be performed mentally or by hand is not enough (see discussion that combining may be 'add[ing] and averag[ing]'). Also note BSG Tech: use of the ineligible concept cannot supply the inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent challenger must overcome the presumption of validity; courts recognize that a challenger must establish ineligibility by clear and convincing evidence, though courts are not required to defer to Patent Office determinations as to eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge Microsoft v. i4i for presumption of validity and the district court note that 'a patent challenger must establish ineligibility by clear and convincing evidence.' Also note Sanderling: courts need not defer to PTO eligibility conclusions.
